The route is unroped scrambling throughout, but the connecting ledge is in places only about a foot wide with steep exposure, passes under a small overhang requiring a crawl in one spot, and can hold snow and require an ice axe/crampons into mid-August.
overview: Greenwood Mountain's standard line follows its West Ridge, reached via a long, exposed connecting ledge from neighboring Dumbell Mountain; it is an unroped talus-and-scree scramble almost always climbed together with Dumbell in a single trip staged from upper Phelps Basin.

current.approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, Wenatchee River Ranger District), follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north, entering the Glacier Peak Wilderness at 2.6 miles, to Spider Meadow (about 4.5-5 miles from the trailhead). Continue past Spider Meadow on the climbers' path, staying right of the tumbling creek to scramble up slabs past waterfalls, then continue up grass, talus, and heather slopes trending northeast into upper Phelps Basin. A commonly used bivy sits around 5,700-5,800 ft near treeline with stream access (the basin above 6,000 ft often has only snow-patch camping). In upper Phelps Basin the trail fades; in late July staying climbers-left to about 5,800 ft, then turning right toward the main drainage under Dumbell, worked well, and a bootpath beside that gully shows in early September. The access road is rocky, so bring some clearance.
current.descent: Descend the West Ridge talus back to the Dumbell-Greenwood col, then carefully reverse the narrow connecting ledge around Dumbell's east face to the ~7,900 ft notch above the south-side gully. Downclimb the loose Class 2-3 gully/ledges back into upper Phelps Basin; on snow, plunge-stepping or glissading speeds this section when conditions allow. There is no rappel route commonly described for this line — the ledge and gullies are downclimbed. Do not attempt the ledge crossing in the wet; several parties have retreated rather than cross it in rain.
current.detailed_rack: This is an unroped scramble, not a technical rope route — no rock rack is needed for the standard West Ridge line. Some parties carry a short rope as a personal safety margin for the exposed ledge traverse, though it is not commonly protected and no fixed anchors are described.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection exists on this route. It is Class 2-3 scrambling with one notably exposed, narrow ledge traverse; parties uncomfortable with unprotected exposure sometimes carry a rope to hand-line the ledge crossing, though most climb it unroped.

name: Groove Thang
beta: Climbs the big, blocky groove between Just Enough and Notta Slab. Shares its start with Notta Slab, then breaks left into a wide, chimney-like feature after the 2nd bolt. 16 bolts to chain anchors; a 70m rope is needed to lower/toprope the full length, and walkers can also descend from the summit.
overview: One of the newest and longest routes at Megadike North, following the large blocky groove between Just Enough and Notta Slab.

current.approach: From Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, continue ~1.1-1.2 mi to the Megadike North pull-out and approach trail near the culvert.
current.descent: A 70m rope is required to lower the full 105 ft in one stretch; alternatively, climbers reaching the anchor can walk off the ridge crest back down to the base.
current.detailed_rack: 18 quickdraws, 70m rope.
current.pro_needs: 16 bolts to a chain anchor; this is the longest single pitch in the area, so bring a full rack and a 70m rope.

name: Southeast Route
beta: Serious alpine scramble requiring climbing experience and high mountain skills. Follows overgrown logging roads and climbers' trails from Barclay Lake, ascending steeply through forest to boulder field approach. Technical crux is an exposed class 3-4 hidden ramp with loose rock and significant exposure. A narrow ledge on north side of summit requires careful foot placement, especially in wet or icy conditions. Multiple search and rescue incidents have occurred on this peak.
overview: Gunn Peak is an extraordinarily prominent summit above the Sultan Basin and Skykomish valley — the highest point in the Wild Sky Wilderness and the 29th-most prominent peak in Washington, its 3,600-plus feet of prominence making it a coveted objective. First climbed July 18, 1915 by Dr. Harry B. Hinman, Walter Eriksen, and Louis Lesh. The standard route climbs from Barclay Lake Trailhead over Tailgunner Pass into Gunn Basin, then up the southwest corner of the summit block via a hidden, often-wet Class 3 ramp through a lower cliff band (the 'hidden ramp'), squeezing through a notch east of the true summit to exposed heather ledges on the north side leading to the top. Few parties climb it each year, largely due to the brushy, easy-to-lose approach and short but serious summit-block exposure; many combine it with neighboring Tailgunner Peak.

current.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,200 ft, end of FS Rd 6024 out of Baring) do not follow the maintained Barclay Lake Trail #1055; instead walk back down the access road roughly a quarter mile and pick up the old, deactivated Barclay Creek spur road (parties who know the route often park directly at the spur's gated start rather than the main Barclay Lake lot). Follow the old roadbed about 100-200 yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden 'Gunn climbers' path.' The path drops to Barclay Creek and crosses via a log-jam/rock-hop near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island — this ford is the approach's main early-season hazard, since the crossing can run high and slick with spring runoff. On the far bank the boot path swings west then turns north and starts climbing in earnest: about 200 ft of easier grade gives way to sustained, tight switchbacks gaining roughly 1,500 ft through second-growth timber with generally good tree/root holds underfoot but a steep, sometimes loose tread. Around 3,600-3,800 ft the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, a known route-finding trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band in partial shade. A usually-dry waterfall ravine is crossed around 4,400 ft (can carry meltwater and be slick in early season). The trail continues switchbacking up brushy, sometimes slide-alder-choked terrain for another ~1,500 ft to gain the ridge crest at roughly 5,400 ft — call it 3-4 hours and about 3,200 ft of gain above the creek crossing for a fit party. From the ridge crest, drop about 100 ft off the crest to skirt a cliff band, then boulder-hop roughly 500 ft up a talus basin to the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face, which marks the base of the summit scrambling. There is no reliable water above Barclay Creek/the waterfall ravine in late summer, so fill up early. Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus, so route-finding (not technical difficulty) is the main hazard on the upper approach — carrying a GPS track or recent trip-report beta is strongly recommended. In early October the creek is crossed on logs, one of which was rotting at its far end.
approach_variant_names: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — essentially every accessible way off Gunn's summit block funnels back through the same notch, ledge, and ramp used going up, so this is fundamentally a downclimb/walk-off rather than a rappel route, with one optional short rappel commonly used at the crux. From the summit, downclimb the short class 3 blocks back to the notch between the peak's two summit 'horns,' then reverse the narrow, roughly one-foot-wide dirt/heather ledge traversing the north face — this exposed traverse is the route's crux in both directions and is meaningfully more dangerous descending when wet, icy, or snow-covered; less experienced parties should consider a handline here. Below the ledge, downclimb back through the class 3-4 notch move to the 'hidden ramp,' a roughly 10-ft, near-vertical step in the cliff band with two options: a chockstone-choked gully (near class 5) on the left, or a more exposed class 3-4 line to the right. This ramp is the one spot on the peak where parties commonly rappel instead of downclimbing — parties describe a sling/rappel station left on a horn or chockstone here (a natural anchor, not bolted; inspect and back it up before trusting it), and a single rappel of roughly 15-20 m clears the step, so a 30 m rope doubled is more than sufficient. Confident scramblers frequently downclimb this section unroped instead, and some parties opt to rappel the steeper gully just right of the ramp when it is wet, icy, or holding snow rather than the ramp itself. Below the ramp, re-cross the talus basin, regain the boot path, and climb back up to the ridge crest (~5,400 ft) before dropping down the switchbacking forest trail, re-crossing Barclay Creek at the log jam, and following the old spur road back to the Barclay Lake Trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No rock protection needed as this is a scramble, not a rock climbing route. However, carry 1-2 runners/slings and carabiners if planning to use rappel station above hidden ramp section. A 30 m rope is optional but recommended for groups with inexperienced members, as a handline or for the one short rappel at the hidden ramp.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection required for ascent (scramble), but some parties install slings and anchors at hidden ramp crux to facilitate safe descent via rappel. If descending by rappel, ensure anchor integrity before committing weight.
current.rope_note: Standard route is unroped Class 3-4 for competent scramblers; a hand line is sometimes rigged on the exposed 'hidden ramp' descent, and the narrow summit ledge is consequential if wet/icy.

name: Gunnshy Peak Standard Route (Barclay Lake Approach)
beta: There is no official trail to Gunnshy Peak. From a spur road near the Barclay Lake Trailhead, a faint but generally followable climber's path heads east into the forest and leads most of the way to the summit. Along the way parties cross Barclay Creek (log crossing), climb a steep forested headwall to roughly 3,600 ft, drop into and cross a waterfall/stream gully (dry by late summer, medium-to-large flow possible in winter/spring), work through brush and talus past Point 5,760+ near a saddle around 5,360-5,400 ft below Tailgunner (Peak 5,842') and Wing Peak, then either traverse via the Gunn Lake basin (summer/fall) or bypass a rocky buttress on open slopes (winter/spring) to reach the final Class 2-3 summit scramble. Total round trip is roughly 9 miles with 4,300-5,000+ ft of cumulative elevation gain depending on route-finding and how much of the ridge is regained. The route is non-technical but should not be taken for granted — genuine mountaineering skills (route-finding, brush travel, exposed scrambling) are required.
overview: Gunnshy Peak (Peak 6218), the second-highest summit in the Wild Sky Wilderness, is reached by an unmaintained climber's path that leaves the Barclay Lake trailhead spur, crosses Barclay Creek, climbs a steep forested headwall and a seasonal waterfall gully, then follows brushy ridge and basin terrain past the Tailgunner/Wing saddle to a short, exposed Class 2-3 scramble on the summit block.

current.approach: From Monroe, drive east on US-2 to the town of Baring. Near milepost 41-42, across from a convenience store, turn left (north) onto 635th Place NE. Cross the railroad tracks and continue about 0.3 mile to a junction; keep left on 635th Place NE for another 0.1 mile, where the road becomes Forest Road 6024 (Barclay Creek Road). Continue roughly 3.9-4.3 miles of gravel forest road (watch for potholes and rough patches; AWD/4x4 recommended after wet weather) to the Barclay Lake Trailhead (vault toilet on site, parking for roughly 20 vehicles, Northwest Forest Pass required). From a spur road near the trailhead, follow the spur toward an old fire pit, where a faint, mostly-unmarked climber's path heads east into the forest and begins the ascent proper. Partway up the steep forested section the path can seem to stop at a gully; the continuing bootpath leaves to the climber's left, and the gully itself goes only at greater difficulty.
approach_variant_names: Barclay Lake spur road to the east ridge
current.descent: There is no separate descent route; parties retrace the ascent. The steep, brushy headwall and the waterfall gully crossing are the two sections most worth downclimbing carefully and in daylight — wet rock in the gully and loose footing on the headwall are the main hazards on the way down. In early season or after fresh snow, the open slopes above the saddle and the bypass around Point 5,760+ can be icy or avalanche-prone; reversing this section requires the same care as the ascent.
current.detailed_rack: This is a non-technical scramble route; no roped protection rack is used or needed on the standard line.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is placed on the standard route — it is a Class 2-3 scramble typically climbed without a rope. A helmet for rockfall/loose rock, sturdy scrambling boots, and trekking poles for the steep brushy sections are the essential kit rather than any rack.

name: Gunrunner
beta: Traverse all four major summits on north-facing ascents and south-facing descents. Features 18 pitches of mostly new climbing: three pitches of 5.10 crack climbing with one aid point used to escape a dead-end fist crack near North Peak summit. Rappel descent includes free-hanging rappel over moat onto Blue Glacier in darkness.
overview: A major traverse connecting all four Gunsight peaks (Northeast, North, Middle, South), offering sustained alpine crack climbing on excellent granite with breathtaking remote alpine positioning.

current.approach: Middle Peak shares the same approach as South Peak: from Downey Creek Trailhead, follow the southern Ptarmigan Traverse cross-country route (Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake, Bachelor Creek) to reach the range's ridge. Expect a multi-day glaciated approach with route-finding and bushwhacking, not a drive-up or short-trail access.
approach_variant_names: Downey Creek, Bachelor Creek and Itswoot Ridge
Stehekin, Agnes Creek and the Blue Glacier
current.descent: The traverse climbs the north faces of the four Gunsight summits and rappels their south sides. From South Peak, a rappel descent leads to the Blue Glacier; the last rappel is free-hanging over a gaping moat onto the glacier, so look for the line that clears it. Check every rappel anchor on the granite thoroughly before trusting it. Parties often finish this descent in darkness. The rappels land on the east side of the range: a party camped below the Blue Glacier walks down to camp, while one based at the Dome-Chickamin col must work south below the peaks, cross the Blizzard-Gunsight col back onto the Chickamin Glacier, and recross the glacier to the col. Allow 3-4 hours, depending on snow and crevasse conditions on the glacier.
current.detailed_rack: Full range of cracks and aid rack recommended: 1-2x each of 0.3-1.5 inch Alien or TC Pro cams, complete medium-sized stopper set, hexes for medium-sized placements, 0.5-1 inch pitons for aid, 2-3 slings of various sizes, 2-3 quickdraws, carabiners, cordelette for rappel anchors.
rack: 5-6 slings plus tat/webbing for sparse fixed anchors
Single dynamic rope for climbing; carry two ropes for the rappel descent (per route beta)
current.pro_needs: Full trad rack required. Splitter cracks on north faces provide excellent natural protection. Anchors are typically solid granite with bomber placements. Rappel anchors should be redundant and well-tested before weighting. No fixed anchors remain on route.
bivy: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
current.rope_note: Part of the Gunsight Peaks Traverse (IV 5.10 A1) crossing all four Gunsight summits; encounters three pitches of 5.10 crack climbing on remote, rarely-visited rock. Confirmed via a trip report (FA by Blake Herrington and Dan Hilden).

name: Improbable Traverse
beta: Start from Alpental parking lot and reach the talus cone by a line that avoids the private Strasse roads (no established path). Scramble ~200 feet of loose, mossy, dirty slabs to reach first anchor. Climb 6 pitches of mixed alpine rock through crumbly terrain to Lunch Ledge at ~300 feet. The iconic traverse (pitches 4-5) traverses right on good ledges with old fixed pitons; now requires careful downclimbing due to 2021 damage. Upper pitches climb Class 4 ramp terrain with trees and exposure to summit. Route is sustained and exposed throughout; not a beginner alpine rock climb.
overview: A technical alpine rock climb on Guye Peak's prominent west face offering a classic 5.8 traverse pitch with stellar views from Interstate 90. Once popular, the route was heavily damaged by rockfall in November 2021; current conditions are marginal and downclimbing on the traverse is now required.

current.approach: From Alpental Ski Area parking lot (3,120 ft), reach the talus cone below the west face by a line that stays off the private Alpental Community Club roads; the 'Strasse' roads off the access road are closed to walking and driving, and no established path exists. Approach time ~30 minutes to 1 hour from parking. In early August a public roadside pullout just past the private Strasse entrance serves as parking; keep to the left side of the talus where the rock is less loose.
approach_variant_names: Talus cone below the west face
current.descent: After summiting via Improbable Traverse, most climbers traverse north over Guye's north and middle summits to descend via established gully systems. A climbers' trail descends from the Guye-Snoqualmie saddle area. For faster/safer descent, fixed anchors (tree with rap tatters) provide rappel opportunity on east side of summit to bypass exposure. Southeast Couloir descent toward Cave Ridge parking is viable alternative.
current.detailed_rack: Mid-size alpine rock rack with 6-8 cams and nuts (mostly cams for Guye's crumbly rock); 60-meter rope minimum (bring two ropes for safe rappel options); full rack of medium to large chocks; several double runners or slings for extending placements around flakes.
current.pro_needs: Protection is generally intermittent and poor-quality due to loose flakes and crumbly rock. Many dirt-filled cracks yield marginal placements. Several old fixed pitons remain on the traverse pitch itself. Plan for lots of sling extensions around features rather than clean gear placements. Tree anchors available for rappel.

name: West Face
beta: From Alpental parking, make a rising traverse up talus to the far left (north) side of the west face (note private road access restrictions as of 2021). Ascend a very large ramp that traverses the entire face from north to south. The climbing starts up a steep crack/face (crux) for approximately 30 feet of low 5th class, then transitions to Class 4 for about half a rope length through rocks and alpine trees with exposure. Climbing continues via mixed scrambling and rock sections to the summit. Route involves significant high-consequence scrambling.
overview: Guye Peak's west face rises above the Alpental valley at Snoqualmie Pass. This is its easiest line and a short, close-to-the-road alpine outing: from the north end of the talus it follows a huge tree-covered ramp that climbs across the whole face from north to south, then a short step of Class 4 to low fifth onto a second grassy ramp, and a final low-fifth crack and face that eases through rock and alpine trees to the south summit. The rock is often dirty and loose. The harder Improbable Traverse on the same face is a separate climb.

current.approach: From the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,100-3,120 ft, I-90 Exit 52), make your way to the talus cone below the west face. There is no established path to it: the old direct line up through the houses on the 'Strasse' roads crosses private land the Alpental Community Club has closed to walkers since 2021, so pick a line that stays off those roads. On the talus, make a rising traverse toward the north end of the large, unstable talus field below the west face — helmet on here, since climber-triggered rockfall is a real hazard on this talus, both from your own party and anyone above. Near the north end of the talus you'll cross a rocky streambed that's often dry by mid-to-late summer (your last realistic water before the climb). From there it's a short scramble up broken rock/slab to the base of the West Face route proper. Total approach is around 1.5 miles and 1,500-2,000 ft of gain, roughly 45 minutes to 1.5 hours depending on conditions and pace.
approach_variant_names: Talus cone below the west face
current.descent: West Face tops out on Guye's south summit (where the route tops out and the register sits; GPS surveys suggest the north summit may be marginally higher) at ~5,169-5,172 ft alongside the middle and north summits, and the descent is a scramble/rappel traverse north along the connecting ridge rather than a reversal of the climbing line. From the south summit, follow the climber's path around the east (right) side of the middle summit to the notch beyond the middle summit. The drop into the gully here is loose, mossy class 3/4 slab; most parties rappel rather than downclimb it. The total rappelling on this route comes to roughly 100 ft, enough that many groups get by with an arm-wrap/hip rappel off a sling rather than a full rap setup, though bringing a rope and device is still the sane default. Important: there is a tree at the top of the gully between the south and middle summits that climbers should specifically NOT rappel from (flagged as unsound/inadvisable in route notes) — use the established sling/anchor lower or to the side instead. Past the middle-summit notch, descend the gully and slabs to the right (east side) to go around the north summit, then scramble up an easy gully to the notch on the north summit's north side. From there, a well-defined scrambler's trail leads down past a small pond, then west (left) back to the Alpental parking lot. Bring a single 30m+ rope and rap device even though the raps are short — anchor tat and rock quality are inconsistent year to year, and the loose gully rock is a real hazard for parties above/below each other. Expect 1 rappel as the norm on this route (occasionally a short second one depending on exact line through the middle/north notch), well short of full pitch length.
current.detailed_rack: Light rack of nuts and small to mid-size cams for the short low-fifth crux, plus slings for tree and block anchors
current.pro_needs: Light alpine rack for one short low-fifth crux; slings for tree and block anchors

name: North Route ("Hidden Ridge" variation)
beta: Park at Alpental near the Snow Lake Trailhead and start up the unsigned Cave Ridge/Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail beginning about 100 ft south of the Snow Lake Trail. From a large clearing around 4000-4200 ft, climb to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak, then turn right (south) and follow the ridge to Guye's north summit — class 3 in summer. The 'Hidden Ridge' variation continues from the north summit around an outcropping to a hidden ridge with one 5.4 move (otherwise class 4), rappelling ~30 ft off a slung horn to the notch between the north and middle summits; this was found to be a more direct, more enjoyable line than the standard gully descent in winter/spring conditions.
overview: The north side of Guye Peak is reached via the separate Cave Ridge Trail rather than the West Face talus approach, and is best known as the 'North Route' — a class 3-4 scramble to the north summit that is also run as a scrambling-course objective, not a sustained roped rock climb. A short optional 'Hidden Ridge' variation near the north/middle notch adds one 5.4 move protected by a single ~30 ft rappel off a slung horn. This is measurably easier, and approached differently, than the 5.6-5.8 technical rib route on Guye Peak; the class 3-4 scramble description is consistent across accounts.

current.approach: The documented north-side line to Guye Peak leaves from the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,080-3,120 ft) via the separate, unsigned Cave Ridge/Snoqualmie Mountain boot path, which splits off about 100 ft south of the Snow Lake Trail sign — this is a different trailhead path than the West Face/Improbable Traverse talus approach. Follow it up to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak (roughly 1.5 miles, reported around 4,500-4,600 ft). From the saddle, turn right (south) and follow the ridge toward Guye's north summit; the standard line follows a steep gully system rated class 3 in summer. Climber-triggered rockfall is common on the talus and gully sections, so a helmet is worth wearing once off-trail. A short 'Hidden Ridge' variation near the north summit traverses right to an outcropping where a horn can be slung for a single ~30 ft rappel into the north/middle notch, adding one 5.4 move of class 4/low-5th climbing.
approach_variant_names: Cave Ridge saddle from Alpental
current.descent: The North Route tops out on the same summit ridge system as Guye's other routes, so the descent is the standard south-to-north traverse/rappel sequence rather than a reversal of the climbing line. From the summit reached, scramble/downclimb toward the notch between the middle and north summits, where fixed rappel rings are already slung/bolted into the rock — enough parties found the step steep enough to rig it permanently that a rope-assisted descent (roughly 30-40 ft, single strand or doubled off a shorter rope) is the norm rather than the exception. If your line tops out further south, you'll first need to negotiate the notch between the south and middle summits, which is loose mossy class 3/4 slab commonly rappelled off tree-sling anchors (30-60 ft). A related variation sometimes climbed on this side of the peak, the 'Hidden Ridge' line, itself uses a short 30-40 ft rappel mid-route (leaving the rope in place and top-roping back up), which can add confusion about anchor locations if you're relying on other parties' beta — the rap rings at the middle/north notch are the ones relevant to a normal summit-to-car descent. From the north summit, follow the well-defined scrambler's trail down past a small pond, then swing west back to the Alpental lot. Carry a single 30m+ rope, rap device, and a prussik/cordelette to back up any weathered slings; expect climber-triggered rockfall risk in the gullies, worse when snow patches remain into early summer (the steep gullies here can hold snow into a normal season and feel considerably more serious with snow in them than the bare-rock class 3 of summer conditions).
current.detailed_rack: No rack needed for the standard scramble; webbing/cordelette to sling a horn and a rope for the optional single ~30 ft rappel.
current.pro_needs: No technical rack for the scramble line; webbing to back up the rappel horn on the optional 5.4 variation.

name: Southeast Gully
beta: A Grade II snow climb and the steepest of Guye's gully lines. The angle runs about 45 degrees for the first few hundred feet, then gets progressively steeper the higher you go, reaching roughly 70 degrees near the top. It finishes at the ridge separating the true and false summits. About half the gully sits in shade and half in sun, which the first-ascent party found gave pretty solid snow under the surface - a useful characteristic that also means conditions can differ markedly between the two halves on a warm day. Protection is minimal: an ice axe is mandatory and crampons are required, a picket and rope are suggested (a 50m is preferred over a 30m), rock protection is scarce in peak season, and slung trees provide occasional belays. This is a route where good snow makes it straightforward and bad snow makes it seriously exposed.
overview: A 1,400-foot snow gully on Guye's southeast side that starts at a mellow 45 degrees and steepens steadily to about 70 degrees before topping out on the ridge between the true and false summits.

current.approach: Start from the Pacific Crest Trail North (Snoqualmie Pass North) trailhead, just off I-90 exit 52. Follow the old Commonwealth Basin trail north for approximately 1.4 miles, until Guye Peak lies directly west or northwest of you. From there head straight upslope - the gully initiates directly above. The approach is on maintained trail or, in winter, on whatever bootpack exists, and is short by Cascade standards; the difficulty is judging the snow on the slope between the trail and the base of the gully, which is itself avalanche terrain on a loaded day.
approach_variant_names: Old Commonwealth Basin trail to a bearing of 290 degrees, then straight up
current.descent: Do not plan on downclimbing the gully; at 70 degrees near the top with minimal protection it is a bad retreat. From the ridge between the true and false summits, the standard exit is over the top and out on foot. Going west, drop from the Guye / Cave Ridge saddle onto the climbers' trail down to the Alpental parking area, which then leaves a road walk of roughly a mile back to a car parked on the Commonwealth side. Going east, reverse the Commonwealth Basin approach back to the PCT North trailhead, which is the natural choice if that is where you left the car. In winter both descents cross avalanche terrain of their own, and the west-side bootpath is easily lost under snow - carry a track or a bearing.
current.detailed_rack: Deliberately light. A picket and a rope are suggested - a 50m is preferred over a 30m - and slung trees provide the occasional belay on the flanks. Rock protection is minimal during peak season, so do not plan a rack around it: bring a few slings and a couple of nuts if you want them; most of this route is climbed with the axe and your feet.
current.pro_needs: Minimal. A picket, a few slings for trees, and the acceptance that much of the 70-degree upper gully is effectively unprotected.

name: Cougar Divide Route
beta: From the Cougar Divide Trailhead (~4,900 ft), the unmaintained Cougar Divide Trail #601 climbs along a ridge crest through meadows and old growth to its high point near 5,920 ft (about 3.1 miles in). From there the route continues cross-country along the open ridge, crossing toward Dobbs Cleaver/Chowder Ridge, to merge with the Skyline Divide approach below Hadley Peak's northwest ridge. The final push to the summit is Class 2 with a brief Class 3 step over loose scree, with generally mild exposure for experienced scramblers.
overview: A shorter, higher-starting alternative to the Skyline Divide approach, climbing the Cougar Divide ridge trail from the end of FS Road 33 to Chowder Ridge before joining the same Class 2 scramble to Hadley Peak's summit.

current.approach: From Glacier, WA, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east and turn onto Forest Service Road 33; follow roughly 11 miles of gravel road (rough in sections, high-clearance/SUV recommended, sedans passable with care) to its end at the Cougar Divide Trailhead/parking (room for 8-10 vehicles). Note the true trailhead may be roughly another kilometer past where online mapping apps route. Hike Cougar Divide Trail #601 along the ridge to its high point (~5,920 ft), then continue cross-country south along the open ridge to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley Peak's final scramble.
approach_variant_names: Cougar Divide Trail #601 and the open ridge south to Chowder Ridge
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the short Class 3 step and loose scree back onto the connecting ridge, then retrace the cross-country ridge traverse back to the Cougar Divide Trail's high point (~5,920 ft). Follow the unmaintained Cougar Divide Trail #601 back down through meadows and forest to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: None — this is a non-technical class 2-3 scramble with no roped climbing; no rack, rope, or protection is used.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection or rope is used on the standard scramble line; an ice axe is the main security item carried, useful for residual snow on the ridge in early or late season.
bivy: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge

name: Skyline Divide Route
beta: From the Skyline Divide Trailhead, a rugged, eroded trail switchbacks through forest to the ridge crest at about 2 miles, then rolls over a series of knolls along the open crest to the trail's high point (~6,563 ft) at about 4.5 miles. From there the maintained tread fades into a boot-packed path that continues along the open ridge crest for roughly another 3 miles, crossing minor ups and downs on Chowder Ridge, before reaching the base of Hadley Peak's final scramble. The last push is Class 2 with a short Class 3 step, climbing loose scree and talus to the summit; exposure is generally minimal for experienced parties.
overview: The more popular of Hadley Peak's two standard approaches, following the well-known Skyline Divide trail up onto the ridge crest and then continuing cross-country along Chowder Ridge to the base of Hadley's summit block for a long, scenic ridge-walk scramble.

current.approach: From Glacier, WA, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 1 mile past the Glacier Public Service Center to Glacier Creek Road (FS 39); turn right, then take an immediate left onto Deadhorse Road (FS 37). FS 37 normally continues 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide Trailhead. FS 37 has been closed by the 2021 flood washout at milepost 3.1, and during the repair work it is gated near its start (mile 0.03), so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle; check the road's status before planning around it. When open, hike Skyline Divide Trail #678 through old-growth forest switchbacks and into meadows on the ridge crest (~2 mi), follow the crest to the trail's high point (~6,563 ft, ~4.5 mi), then continue cross-country along the open ridge to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley Peak.
approach_variant_names: Skyline Divide Trail #678 and the long open ridge south to Chowder Ridge
current.descent: From the summit, carefully downclimb the short Class 3 step and the loose scree/talus below it back to the base of the summit block. Retrace the boot-packed path along Chowder Ridge and the open ridge crest (roughly 3 miles) back to the trail's high point (~6,563 ft), then descend the maintained Skyline Divide Trail #678 through meadows and forest switchbacks to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: None — this is a non-technical class 2-3 scramble with no roped climbing; no rack, rope, or protection is used.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection or rope is used on the standard scramble line; the main 'gear' concern is footing on loose rock and residual snow, for which an ice axe is recommended in early or late season.
bivy: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge

name: Hail Satan
beta: Fully bolted (8 bolts) single-pitch sport route starting from a ledge about 25 feet off the ground; features small intrusions used as footholds/handholds on otherwise blank-looking granite. Low traffic and lightly documented — expect an adventurous, quiet outing.
overview: A short, punchy single-pitch sport line up balancy friction and face holds on the broad arete forming the right side of the Mamie Peak crag.

current.approach: This crag's coordinates correspond to the Hannegan Pass/Ruth Creek Valley area near Mt. Baker, sometimes referenced as 'Ellation Crags,' a minor, lightly-developed granite cragging/multipitch area. The general access is from I-5 Exit 255, east on SR-542 (Mt. Baker Highway) about 46 miles, then a left onto Forest Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road) for about 4 miles to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead. Beyond that trailhead, published approach details for the crag itself are sparse and inconsistent, so the exact on-foot route and distance are not confirmed.
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the single pitch back to the base of the crag; a standard single rope reaches the ground from the anchor. Retrace the brushy climbers' path back down to the Hannegan Pass Trail and out to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted; no natural gear required.
current.pro_needs: 8 bolts to a fixed anchor — bring 8-10 quickdraws.
